# Constant and rechargeable cells (Daniell, lead-acid, dry cell) (`practical_batteries`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: needs electric_battery; helped by sulphuric_acid, zinc_brass, electrolysis
- Core idea: Volta's pile fades because hydrogen collects on the copper. The Daniell cell avoids this: zinc in dilute sulphuric acid or zinc sulphate, copper in a saturated solution of copper sulphate (blue vitriol), the two liquids kept apart by a porous unglazed pot. It gives a steady 1.1 volts for days and made telegraphy possible. Two lead plates in dilute sulphuric acid form a cell that can be charged from another source and gives the current back at about 2 volts (lead-acid accumulator). Zinc and a carbon rod packed in manganese dioxide, with sal ammoniac solution, give 1.5 volts and, made as a paste, the dry cell.
- Pitfalls:
  - Letting the two solutions of a Daniell cell mix: copper plates out on the zinc and the cell dies
  - Charging a lead cell in a closed room or near a flame: it gives off hydrogen, which explodes
  - Confusing voltage with capacity: more cells in series raise the voltage, larger plates give more current for longer
  - Impurities in zinc cause corrosion even on open circuit. Historical cells used mercury amalgamation, which introduces a toxic metal. High-purity zinc reduces local corrosion
- History: europe: 1836 – Daniell cell (London); 1839 Grove cell; 1859 Planté lead-acid accumulator, 1881 Faure pasted plates; 1866 Leclanché cell; 1886 Gassner dry cell
- Read:
  - J. Frederic Daniell, On Voltaic Combinations, Philosophical Transactions 126 (1836)
  - Richard H. Schallenberg, Bottled Energy: Electrical Engineering and the Evolution of Chemical Energy Storage (1982)
